It adopts digital technologies including mixed reality (MR) blending virtual overdose scenarios with physical surroundings, the Apple Vision Pro spatial-computing headset, the Unity game engine, hand-movement detection for simulated 911 calls, haptic feedback, immersive video, and MR spatial computing. It captures tacit knowledge such as opioid-overdose recognition, CPR and naloxone-response skills, calling 911, checking breathing, administering intranasal naloxone, behavioral preparedness, confidence in rescue breathing/chest compressions/naloxone administration, intent to intervene, muscle memory, and situational awareness. The practice depends on organizational dependencies (person trained to operate the headset, downloaded application, Illinois Innovation Network funding) and environmental dependencies (diverse physical location constraints). It is constrained by limitations including the gap between knowledge gains and real-world intervention, need for additional practice, variability in digital literacy, uncertain long-term retention, insufficient evidence of equivalence to in-person training, absence of mannequin-like tactile feedback, interface problems, physical-space constraints, single-user per device, headset discomfort, device cost, and need for refresher training. The mechanism is that ReviveXR uses MR and spatial computing to provide immersive, self-paced, haptic-feedback-driven training that transfers and captures tacit overdose-response skills, while being dependent on trained personnel, downloaded software, funding, and physical space, and facing limitations in tactile feedback, scalability, and long-term skill retention.
